chunks.text:
## Acne care principles
Mild acne care is gentle: a non-harsh cleanser twice a day, an oil-free or gel moisturizer, daily sunscreen, and one proven acne ingredient such as salicylic acid, benzoyl peroxide, adapalene or azelaic acid. Results take six to eight weeks, so give a routine time before changing it.

## Common mistakes
Over-washing, scrubbing, picking pimples and using many strong actives together damage the skin barrier and often make acne and redness worse. Skipping moisturizer on oily skin can also increase oil and irritation.

## Blackheads and whiteheads
Blackheads and whiteheads (closed comedones) are clogged pores. Salicylic acid, adapalene and azelaic acid are commonly used. Regular gentle exfoliation a few times a week can help. Squeezing causes scarring.

## Post-acne marks
Dark marks after pimples fade slowly over months. Daily sunscreen is the most important step. Ingredients such as niacinamide, azelaic acid, vitamin C and tranexamic acid are commonly used. Do not pick spots, as it makes marks darker.

## When acne needs a doctor
Painful deep cysts or nodules, scarring, acne that covers large areas, or acne that does not improve after two to three months of consistent gentle care should be seen by a dermatologist. Prescription treatments should only be started under medical advice.

## Signs of a damaged barrier
A damaged skin barrier can cause stinging, tightness, flaking, redness, sudden sensitivity to products that were fine before, and more breakouts. It often follows over-exfoliation or using too many actives.

## Repairing the barrier
Simplify the routine: use a gentle cleanser, a ceramide or barrier-repair moisturizer and sunscreen. Pause exfoliating acids, retinoids and vitamin C until the skin feels normal again, which can take two to four weeks.

## Helpful barrier ingredients
Ceramides, cholesterol, fatty acids, panthenol (vitamin B5), glycerin, hyaluronic acid, centella and niacinamide help support the barrier. Thick balms can be used at night.

## Dehydrated skin versus dry skin
Dry skin lacks oil and tends to be flaky and rough. Dehydrated skin lacks water and can be oily yet feel tight and dull. Humectants like hyaluronic acid and glycerin help dehydration, sealed in with a moisturizer.

## Patch testing
Before using a new product on the face, apply a small amount behind the ear or on the inner forearm once a day for three days. Stop if there is itching, swelling or redness.

## Niacinamide
Niacinamide (vitamin B3) helps with excess oil, enlarged-looking pores, uneven tone and a weak skin barrier. It suits most skin types, including oily and acne-prone skin. A small number of people feel mild flushing or tingling at high strengths, so start slowly and patch test.

## Salicylic acid (BHA)
Salicylic acid is an oil-soluble exfoliant that goes inside pores. It helps with blackheads, whiteheads and oily skin. It can dry or irritate, so use it a few times a week at first and do not stack it with other strong exfoliants. Not ideal for very dry or very sensitive skin.

## Azelaic acid
Azelaic acid helps with post-acne marks, uneven tone and mild redness or breakouts. It is usually gentler than many other actives, but it can sting at first. Introduce slowly.

## Vitamin C
Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps with dullness and the look of dark marks. It works best in the morning under sunscreen. Some people find it irritating, so patch test and begin with a few days a week.

## Ceramides
Ceramides are skin-identical fats that help repair and support the skin barrier. They suit dry, sensitive and irritated skin and are safe to use every day with almost any other ingredient.

## Hyaluronic acid
Hyaluronic acid attracts water and helps dehydrated skin feel plumper. It works best on slightly damp skin and should be sealed in with a moisturizer.

## Glycolic acid and other AHAs
AHAs such as glycolic and lactic acid exfoliate the skin surface and help with rough texture and dullness. They increase sun sensitivity, so sunscreen is essential. They can irritate sensitive skin and should not be combined with retinoids or BHAs on the same night.

## Retinoids
Retinol, retinal and adapalene help with texture, clogged pores and early signs of ageing. They cause dryness and peeling at first (called retinization). Use at night, start two nights a week, and always use sunscreen the next day. Avoid combining with exfoliating acids. Not for pregnancy unless a doctor advises.

## Benzoyl peroxide
Benzoyl peroxide reduces acne-causing bacteria and helps inflamed pimples. It can dry the skin and bleach fabrics. Start with a low strength, use it on affected areas or as a short-contact wash, and moisturize well.

## Centella asiatica (cica)
Centella extract is used to soothe and calm redness-prone and irritated skin. It is generally well tolerated and suits sensitive skin.

## Tranexamic acid, arbutin and kojic acid
These ingredients are used for the appearance of dark spots and uneven tone. Results are slow and need daily sunscreen. Patch test, and avoid stacking several brightening actives at once.

## Zinc and sulfur
Zinc and sulfur are used in products for oily and blemish-prone skin to help control shine. They can be drying for some people.

## Simple morning routine
A basic morning routine has three steps: a gentle cleanser (or just water if the skin is very dry), a moisturizer, and a sunscreen. An antioxidant serum such as vitamin C or a niacinamide serum can go between cleanser and moisturizer.

## Simple evening routine
An evening routine is cleanser, one treatment if needed, and moisturizer. If you wore sunscreen or makeup, cleanse well. Treatments such as retinoids, exfoliating acids and azelaic acid are usually used at night.

## Order of products
Apply products from thinnest to thickest: cleanser, toner or essence, serum or treatment, moisturizer, then sunscreen last in the morning.

## Starting a routine as a beginner
Beginners should start with a cleanser, moisturizer and sunscreen only. Add one new active at a time and wait about two weeks before adding another. This makes it easy to find the cause if irritation appears.

## Keeping a routine budget-friendly
Spend the most on sunscreen and on the one treatment that matches your main concern. A cleanser and a moisturizer do not need to be expensive. If a product you already own is gentle and suits your skin, keep using it instead of replacing it.

## Oily skin routine
Oily skin still needs moisture. Use a gel or lightweight cleanser, a gel or oil-free moisturizer, and a light matte or gel sunscreen. Niacinamide or salicylic acid can help control oil.

## Dry skin routine
Dry skin does best with a gentle non-foaming or creamy cleanser, a richer moisturizer with ceramides, and a hydrating sunscreen. Avoid harsh foaming washes and strong acids.

## Combination skin routine
Use a gentle gel cleanser and a lightweight moisturizer. Place stronger oil-control products only on the oily T-zone if the cheeks are dry.

## Sensitive skin routine
Sensitive skin needs a very short routine: gentle cleanser, barrier moisturizer and mineral or gentle sunscreen. Avoid fragrance, strong acids and many active products at once. Patch test every new product.

## Combining strong actives
Do not use several strong actives together, especially on sensitive skin. Retinoids, exfoliating acids (AHA, BHA), benzoyl peroxide and high-strength vitamin C can cause dryness, burning and peeling when stacked. Use one new active at a time, a few nights per week at first.

## Prescription products
Products containing tretinoin, clindamycin, isotretinoin, hydroquinone or steroid creams are medicines. They should be started and monitored by a doctor, not chosen by an app.

## Signs you should see a professional
See a doctor or dermatologist for severe or persistent acne, significant swelling, severe irritation, a suspected allergic reaction, open wounds or bleeding skin, rapidly worsening symptoms, or any problem near the eyes.

## Pregnancy and breastfeeding
Retinoids and some acne medicines are not recommended in pregnancy. Anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding should check skincare ingredients with a doctor.

## Community experiences
Experiences shared by people online are personal stories, not medical evidence. They can help you understand texture or feel of a product but do not prove that a product works for you.

## Why sunscreen matters
Sunscreen is the most important daily step for preventing dark spots, post-acne marks and early ageing. Many brightening and exfoliating products make skin more sun sensitive, so sunscreen is needed when using them. Pakistan has strong UV for much of the year.

## SPF and PA ratings
SPF measures protection against UVB, which causes burning. The PA rating (PA+ to PA++++) shows UVA protection, which causes ageing and pigmentation. For daily use, SPF 30 to 50 with a good UVA rating is enough. Higher numbers add very little extra protection.

## How much and how often
Use about two finger-lengths of sunscreen for the face and neck. Reapply every two to three hours when outdoors for long periods. Indoor daytime use near windows still benefits from sunscreen.

## Choosing sunscreen by skin type
Oily and acne-prone skin usually prefers gel, fluid, milk or matte finishes. Dry skin usually prefers cream or hydrating sunscreens. Sensitive skin often tolerates mineral (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) sunscreens well. Sun sticks are handy for reapplication.

## Mineral and chemical sunscreen
Mineral sunscreens sit on top of the skin and are often gentler for sensitive skin, but can leave a white cast. Chemical sunscreens absorb UV and usually feel lighter, but a few people find them stinging, especially near the eyes.
